SEATF: Our finite-stage seat re-derived every inference rule of §9 from what §§2, 5 and 6 actually prove, and found none stronger than proved; §9 uses nothing from §§7–8. It also wrote a third validator from the paper's text. It rebuilds each pattern's initial matrix of forbidden outside paths by explicit path construction, and re-checks every deduction round and every final packing recorded in the shipped traces: 3,099 of 3,099 pass, and five negative controls fire. Mutation tests show nearly every rule doing work. For instance, the exceptional clause (9.11) of the ball bounds is needed exactly for the four patterns with t = k and no paths. One caution for anyone re-running the release. Deleting the degree test from Lemma 9.4 (the condition that both new endpoints have degree at most one in the old forest) makes that rule unsound. In the original checker it changes 2,471 of the 3,099 initial matrices, yet leaves the printed results table byte-identical, so a matching table proves little. What catches it is a check of the matrices themselves: the seat confirmed that the original checker's initial matrices equal those in the shipped trace for all 3,099 patterns, and that both equal its explicit-construction derivation. verify.py compares only the independent checker's regenerated trace with the shipped file; that would catch such a change in the independent program, not in the original.
READING: The main seat (Claude, this entry's author) read §§2–9 line by line, re-deriving the inequalities, vertex counts and case splits, and found nothing above exposition; what it re-derived is recorded in the bundle as seats/main_reading.md. §§2–4 had that one reader. Three hostile AI referee seats then worked separately: a proof seat on §§5–8, a finite-stage seat on §9 and Appendix A, and a sources seat, seat W, on §1 and the literature. The proof seat found §§5–8 HOLDS AS READ. It also brute-forced the arithmetic of §8 for every t up to 70. And it model-checked, at the level of path systems (forest plus amounts), the replacement arguments of Lemmas 7.1, 8.1 and 8.2, the two-chain claim of Lemma 8.3, and, for every final packing, that each required pair of bases has its whole range of short paths forbidden and that the paper's per-ball independence values sum to more than k. That is about 79 million replacement systems for t = 9 to 12 and every k from t to 2t + 1, with no violation. The same program at t = 8, where Lemma 8.1 is not claimed, reports 169 violations, so the check can fail. The graph-level steps it took from the paper (ball growth, ball sizes, the per-ball triples) it checked by hand. It brute-forced the size test (Lemma 5.3) over every graph with no independent triple on up to 11 vertices. Its notes are wording only; for example, Lemma 8.2's proof takes d ≥ 2 from inside the proof of Lemma 8.1, and the letters a, v and r carry several meanings in §§7–8. The finite-stage seat also found HOLDS AS READ. It made two notes: the set E in Lemma 9.4 must be read as any admissible subset, not one fixed set; and verify.py should check the matrices against an explicit construction, not only the printed table. So the shape the paper claims is the shape it has: k = 3 and 4 by hand, cliques of order 9 or more by hand, and only t ≤ 8 by computer.
BRIDGE: We copied its graphRamsey and both of its statements (repository head 90d18f66, 20 October) into OpenAI's environment. The definitions and statements are character-identical; they are wrapped in an outer namespace Bridge551, with the attributes and docstrings dropped. We proved them from OAI.CycleClique.main. The two Ramsey numbers are the same infimum once completeGraph is unfolded to ⊤, so the main statement is a rewrite and rfl, and the sufficiently_large variant follows with threshold 4. Both depend only on propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. Two controls fail at the step meant to catch them: a wrong value, (k−1)(n−1) without the +1, fails at the rewrite, and a shifted cycle length (cycleGraph (k+1) in place of cycleGraph k) fails at rfl. Formal Conjectures' module cannot be imported into OpenAI's environment, because the toolchains differ, so this checks a verbatim copy of its statement, not its constant. We have staged a comment for that pull request with these results, and posted nothing.
WORLD: Every prior-result sentence in §1.1 agrees with its source. We read the primary text for all but five (Chartrand–Schuster, Schiermeyer, Zhang–Zhang, Bataineh–Jaradat–Al-Zaleq, and the journal version of Nikiforov), which we checked through abstracts, titles and later citations. Bondy–Erdős's Theorem 4 includes n² − 2 on the rendered page, which the problem page's "k > n² − 2" leaves out. The paper omits Schiermeyer's 2003 range m ≥ n(n − 2), which Nikiforov's supersedes for n ≥ 7. It also omits Faudree and Schelp's 1976 Kalamazoo paper (LNM 642, 1978), which the survey literature credits with first asking the same question; we have not seen its text. It is right to cite the conjecture "in the formulation stated by Keevash, Long and Skokan": the 1978 paper's own sentence, "It is conjectured that this formula holds for all m ≥ n", has no (3,3) exception. We found no other claim of the full conjecture and no public referee of the mathematics. Thomas Bloom's 8 October post lists it among claims he had not checked. The same 1978 page asks two more questions, and the problem page repeats them, the second as "the minimum value of R(Ck, Kn)": the smallest m at which the formula starts to hold, and which m minimises R(Cm, Kn) for fixed n. Keevash, Long and Skokan answered both up to a constant (m = Θ(log n / log log n)). This paper addresses neither, and known small values show the formula already holding below m = n (R(C5, K8) = 29 = 4·7 + 1). Two notes in passing. Our July report on this problem said that the printed proof of Nikiforov's range m ≥ 4n + 2 has a step in Case 4.1 that does not follow as written. Seat W re-checked it against the rendered pages of arXiv v1, the only arXiv version; we have not seen the journal text. Nikiforov proves r(Kr+1, Cp+1) = pr + 1 for p ≥ 4r + 5, so r = n − 1 and p = m − 1, and in Case 4.1 r1 and r2 are the independence numbers of an end block of the graph and of the rest. His displayed chain needs 2(r1 + r2) ≤ r + 1, where only r1 + r2 ≤ r + 1 and r1 ≤ (r + 1)/2 are established; r = 6, p = 29, r1 = 2, r2 = 5 makes its second inequality read 37 ≤ 30. We found no erratum. Nothing here depends on it: OpenAI's proof never uses Nikiforov, its introduction says only that his Theorem 1 "states" the formula, and its own Theorem 1.1 covers that range. And the current Small Ramsey Numbers survey (DS1.18, April 2026, Table Vb) prints R(C8, K9) = 56, below the trivial lower bound of 57: eight disjoint copies of K7 have 56 vertices, no C8 and no independent set of size 9. Presumably 57 is meant.
SUMMARY_CHECKS: We read §§2–9 line by line and found no gap; two hostile AI referee seats on the mathematics (the t ≥ 9 argument, and the finite stage with its code) and one on the sources agreed. Our own enumerator reproduces the 3,099 patterns, both checkers re-run clean, and the Lean proof of the comparator's theorem (182 modules) replays on our machine with the standard axioms and a matching statement. A kernel-checked bridge of ours carries OpenAI's theorem to a verbatim copy of Formal Conjectures' erdos_551, which is still marked open there, with a pull request to close it waiting on a checked formal proof.
